name: Philippine Pangolin
description: The Philippine pangolin is endemic to Palawan and nearby islands. Covered in protective keratin scales, it curls into a ball when threatened and feeds almost exclusively on ants and termites using a long sticky tongue.
habitat: Lowland and mid-elevation forests, secondary growth, and agricultural edges across Palawan.
facts: Endemic to the Palawan faunal region — found nowhere else on Earth.
A single pangolin can eat tens of thousands of ants in one night.
Its scales are made of the same material as human fingernails.

name: Palawan Peacock-Pheasant
description: A stunning ground-dwelling bird endemic to Palawan. Males display iridescent blue-green ocelli on their plumage and perform elaborate courtship dances.
habitat: Primary and secondary lowland forests of Palawan.
diet: Seeds, fruits, insects, and small invertebrates
facts: The national bird of Palawan and a symbol of the province.
Males have metallic blue crests and peacock-like eye spots.
Katala Foundation works to protect its remaining forest habitat.

name: Palawan Hornbill
description: A large black-and-white hornbill found only in Palawan. It plays a vital role as a seed disperser, helping regenerate forest ecosystems.
habitat: Forest canopy from coastal lowlands to foothills.
facts: Pairs seal the female inside a tree cavity while she incubates eggs.
Their loud calls echo through Palawan's forests at dawn.
Critical seed dispersers for large-fruited forest trees.

name: Palawan Bearcat
description: Also known as the binturong, this arboreal mammal has a prehensile tail and a scent often compared to popcorn. The Palawan subspecies is smaller than its mainland relatives.
habitat: Tall forests with dense canopy cover across Palawan.
diet: Fruits (especially figs), small animals, and eggs
facts: One of the few mammals with a fully prehensile tail.
Their musk smells remarkably like buttered popcorn.
Mostly nocturnal and rarely seen in the wild.

name: Palawan Frogmouth
description: A master of camouflage, the Palawan frogmouth sits motionless on branches by day, resembling a broken stump. It hunts insects at night with a wide frog-like gape.
habitat: Forest edges, secondary growth, and wooded gardens.
facts: Nearly invisible during the day thanks to bark-like plumage.
Endemic to the Palawan group of islands.
Named for its broad, frog-like mouth used to scoop insects.

name: Blue-naped Parrot
description: A bright green parrot with a distinctive blue patch on the nape. Once common across the Philippines, wild populations have declined sharply due to trapping for the cage-bird trade.
habitat: Forest, mangroves, coconut plantations, and cultivated areas.
facts: Still relatively common in parts of Palawan compared to other islands.
Often seen in noisy flocks flying between fruiting trees.
Protected under Philippine wildlife law — trapping is illegal.

name: Bakawan Mangrove
description: A keystone mangrove of Palawan’s coasts and estuaries. Tangled stilt roots trap sediment, buffer storms, and create nursery habitat for fish, crabs, and birds.
habitat: Tidal mudflats, river mouths, and sheltered coastal lagoons across Palawan.
facts: Prop roots filter silt and protect shorelines from typhoon surge.
Juvenile fish and crabs use the root tangle as nursery cover.
Palawan’s mangrove belts are critical blue-carbon stores.

name: Narra
description: The Philippines’ national tree — prized for golden hardwood and cascades of yellow blossoms. Still found in lowland forests and planted avenues of Palawan.
habitat: Lowland forest, riverbanks, and open cultivated ground.
facts: National tree of the Philippines.
Flowers briefly carpet the ground in yellow after heavy rains.
Heartwood is durable and historically overharvested.

name: Palawan Pitcher Plant
description: A carnivorous pitcher plant of Palawan’s ultramafic and highland soils. Modified leaves form fluid-filled traps that digest insects where nutrients are scarce.
habitat: Ultramafic hills, mossy forest edges, and nutrient-poor clearings in Palawan.
diet: Photosynthesis plus insects trapped in pitchers
facts: Endemic to Palawan’s specialized soils.
Pitchers lure prey with nectar and color.
Highly sought by collectors — wild harvest is a threat.

name: Ipil
description: A heavy hardwood of coastal and lowland forests, once abundant in Palawan. Slow-growing and heavily logged for construction and boatbuilding.
habitat: Coastal forest, limestone woodland, and near-shore lowland forest.
facts: Timber is extremely dense and rot-resistant.
Often grows near mangroves and beach forest.
Regeneration is slow — recovery needs decades.

name: Talisay
description: A familiar beach-forest tree with broad, layered leaves that turn red before falling. Common along Palawan shores, providing shade and coastal wildlife cover.
habitat: Beaches, coastal strands, and nearshore villages.
facts: Leaves change color seasonally — a rare tropical deciduous display.
Fruits drift on ocean currents, helping the species colonize islands.
Shade tree for nesting shorebirds and resting travelers.

name: Palawan Cycad
description: Ancient seed plants of Palawan’s forests and rocky slopes. Cycads look palm-like but are unrelated — living fossils that predate flowering plants.
habitat: Forest understory, limestone outcrops, and dry hillsides.
facts: Among the oldest seed-plant lineages still alive.
Seeds and leaves are toxic if mishandled.
Slow growth makes wild populations vulnerable to harvest.
